summaryBox.title: Order vs Molecularity
summaryBox.takeaway: Order is an experimental quantity (zero, fraction, integer). Molecularity is a theoretical integer (1, 2, 3) for elementary steps.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
ORDER vs MOLECULARITY
                                     │
         ┌───────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                       ▼
   REACTION ORDER ($n$)                                    MOLECULARITY
   ├── Sum of concentration exponents ($n = x + y$)       ├── Total reacting species colliding
   ├── **Experimental quantity**                          │   simultaneously in an **Elementary Step**
   ├── Can be zero, integer, fraction, or negative        ├── **Theoretical integer** ($1, 2, 3$)
   └── Applies to both elementary and complex pathways    └── Applies strictly to elementary steps
conceptBreakdown.content:
The Rate Law is an experimentally determined mathematical expression relating the reaction rate to the molar concentrations of reactants:
$$\text{Rate} = k [A]^x [B]^y$$
where $k$ is the Rate Constant (Specific Reaction Rate), and $x, y$ are partial reaction orders with respect to $A$ and $B$.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 2.1 Units of Rate Constant (k)
conceptBreakdown.title: 2.1 Units of Rate Constant (k)
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
RATE CONSTANT UNITS BY ORDER
                       
   Zero-Order ($n=0$):     $\text{M}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \text{ or } \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$
   First-Order ($n=1$):    $\text{s}^{-1} \text{ or } \text{min}^{-1}$ (Independent of concentration!)
   Second-Order ($n=2$):   $\text{M}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \text{ or } \text{L}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$
   Third-Order ($n=3$):    $\text{M}^{-2}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \text{ or } \text{L}^2\cdot\text{mol}^{-2}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$
conceptBreakdown.content:
The SI units of the rate constant $k$ depend directly on the overall reaction order $n$:
$$\mathbf{\text{Units of } k = (\text{M})^{1-n} \cdot \text{s}^{-1} = (\text{mol/L})^{1-n} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}}$$

quickRevision: Order n = x + y is experimentally determined.
Molecularity is theoretical (1, 2, 3) for elementary steps.
For first-order, units of k are s⁻¹ (independent of concentration).
